subject: biology
title: Required practical: using a light microscope
key_idea: In this practical you prepare a stained slide, focus a light microscope from low power to high power, and draw the cells you see. You then calculate the magnification of your drawing. Each step in the method has a reason you must be able to give.

blocks.text: Onion epidermis is a common specimen. This section covers the equipment, the method and the reason for each step.

items.meaning: The thing you are looking at, such as a layer of onion cells.
A dye, such as iodine, that makes parts of a cell easier to see.
A thin square of glass or plastic placed over the specimen.

items: Equipment: microscope slide, cover slip, stain, mounted needle, pipette or dropper, scalpel, forceps.
A named stain can be iodine, methylene blue or eosin.
For cheek cells, collect the cells with a swab.

items.text: Cut it into pieces with a sharp knife, on a chopping board.
A thin layer lets light pass through, so individual cells can be seen.
Put the layer flat on the microscope slide.
Add a few drops of iodine solution. It stains the cell so the nucleus and other parts can be seen.
Lower it at an angle. This reduces air bubbles and keeps the specimen flat and in place.

rows: May cause an allergic reaction or skin rash
Wear gloves, use a dropper bottle and wash skin straight away after contact
May cut you or someone else
Cut away from the body, on a chopping board, with fingers away from the blade

items: A thin layer lets light through. A stain shows the parts of the cell.
Lower the cover slip at an angle to reduce air bubbles.
Name the hazard, the risk and a way to reduce it.

blocks.text: Always start on the lowest power. Then increase the magnification step by step.

diagram.alt: Put the steps for preparing and viewing an onion cell slide in the correct order.
steps: Peel a thin layer of cells from the onion
Place the layer flat on a microscope slide
Add a few drops of iodine solution
Lower a cover slip over the cells at an angle
Place the slide on the stage
Select the lowest power objective lens
Use the focusing knob to bring the cells into focus
Change to a higher power objective lens and refocus

items: Switch the lamp on, or adjust the mirror, so light passes through the slide.
Start with the lowest power objective lens. It has the widest field of view and is easier to focus.
Move the stage close to the lens without letting the slide touch the lens.
Turn the focusing knob so the slide moves **away** from the lens until the cells are in focus.
Never focus by moving the lens towards the slide: this can damage the lens or the slide.

blocks.label: Total magnification
blocks.formula: total magnification = eyepiece lens magnification × objective lens magnification
where: For example, ×10 eyepiece and ×40 objective give ×400.

blocks.text: If no cells can be seen

items: The slide is not in the correct position, or there are no cells in the field of view.
The mirror or light is not set correctly.
The objective lens is not clicked into place, or is dirty.
You are looking at an air bubble, or the microscope is not focused.
It is more difficult to focus.
The field of view is smaller.
Start with the lowest power objective lens, then change to a higher power and refocus.
Turn the focusing knob so the slide moves away from the lens.
Total magnification = eyepiece × objective.

blocks.text: You draw what you see, label it and show the magnification.

items: Use a sharp pencil and draw clear, continuous lines. Do not shade.
Draw the cells large, so the detail is clear.
Label the parts using ruled lines that do not cross.
Write the magnification beside the drawing.

blocks.label: Magnification of a drawing
blocks.formula: magnification = size of drawing ÷ real size
where: Both sizes in the same unit, such as mm.

items.text: A bacterium is 0.005 mm long. The drawing is 80 mm long.
The drawing has a magnification of ×16 000.

items: A scientific drawing has clear lines, no shading and ruled label lines.
Show the magnification on the drawing.
Magnification = size of drawing ÷ real size.

checks.q: Give a reason why a thin layer of onion cells is used.
checks.a: To allow light to pass through the cells, so individual cells can be seen.

checks.q: Explain why you start with the lowest power objective lens.
checks.a: It has the widest field of view, so the cells are easier to find and focus.

checks.q: A drawing of a bacterium is 80 mm long. The real bacterium is 0.005 mm long. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.

worked_example.question: A student prepared some onion cells. The student peeled off a thin layer of onion epidermis, placed it on a slide, added three drops of iodine solution, and lowered a cover slip at an angle. Give a reason for each of the following steps in the method. A thin layer of onion epidermis is used. Iodine solution is added to the onion epidermis. The cover slip is lowered onto the onion epidermis at an angle.
answer_points: Thin layer: to help see individual cells, so light can penetrate.
Iodine solution: to stain, so the parts of the cell can be seen (for example the nucleus, cytoplasm or cell wall).
Cover slip at an angle: to prevent or reduce air bubbles.
worked_example.tip: One mark for each reason. "To stain the cell" on its own is ignored.

worked_example.question: A student took a sample of cells from a meristem to view under a light microscope. Describe how the student would prepare a microscope slide using these cells.
answer_points: Use a thin section of the cells (or meristem).
Add a stain (or a named stain).
Place a cover slip on top of the sample.
worked_example.tip: One mark each. Adding a sample of the cells to the slide is also accepted, and so is describing how to lower the cover slip.

worked_example.question: A student prepares onion cell slides to view under a microscope. A student thinks that using the highest magnification of a microscope is always best. Explain why this may not be true.
answer_points: It is more difficult to focus.
The field of view is smaller.
worked_example.tip: One mark for each problem with using the highest magnification.
